You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Primary Diagnosis: septic shock
  Secondary: heart failure
  Secondary: abscess in the left thigh
  Secondary: osteomyelitis in the pubis
  Secondary: Fournier's syndrome
  Secondary: chronic kidney disease
  Secondary: acute dialysis
  Secondary: cardiorespiratory arrest
  Secondary: hyperkalemia
  Secondary: bradycardia
  Secondary: QRS widening
  Secondary: refractory shock
Symptoms at admission: heart failure; abscess in the left thigh
Anomalies/Findings:
  [ABNORMAL] Norepinephrine infusion = 1.5 mcg/kg/min
  [ABNORMAL] Hyperkalemia (normal: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L)
  [CRITICAL] Cardiorespiratory arrest
  [CRITICAL] Asystole
  [ABNORMAL] Bradycardia
  [ABNORMAL] QRS widening
  [CRITICAL] Refractory shock
  [ABNORMAL] Purulent secretion
  [CRITICAL] Fixed mydriasis
  [CRITICAL] Absence of heart sounds
  [CRITICAL] Absence of brainstem reflexes
  [ABNORMAL] Respiratory rate increased
Procedures performed:
  • Drainage of abscess in left thigh with ultrasound on 12/03
  • Drain placement on 12/15
  • Incision in ICU on 12/17
  • Effective electrical cardioversion on 12/17
  • Dialysis via fistula on 12/16
  • Drainage of Fournier's gangrene on 12/03
  • Intubation on 12/17
  • Cardiopulmonary resuscitation on 12/17
  • Ventilator support on 12/17
Medications:
  • Dobutamine — helps heart pump better | Dosage: 12/07 and 12/08
  • Ceftriaxone — antibiotic to kill bacteria | Dosage: guided by culture of abscess
  • Polymyxin D — antibiotic for resistant bacteria | Dosage: 12/15
  • Amikacin — antibiotic for bacteria | Dosage: 12/17
  • Vancomycin — antibiotic for resistant bacteria | Dosage: 12/17
  • Calcium gluconate — lowes high potassium | Dosage: 2 ampoules
  • Bicarbonate — helps reduce potassium level | Dosage: 100 ml
  • Atropine — stops heart slowing | Dosage: 2 ampoules
  • Norepinephrine — raises blood pressure | Dosage: 1.5 mcg/kg/min
Warning signs to mention:
  ⚠ cardiorespiratory arrest
  ⚠ asystole
  ⚠ absence of central pulses
  ⚠ fixed mydriasis
  ⚠ absence of heart sounds
  ⚠ absence of brainstem reflexes
  ⚠ refractory shock
Hospital stay duration: 14 d 11 h
Outcome: death
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
The patient was admitted on 12/06 and discharged on 12/21 after a stay of 14 days 11 hours in the ward, paid by SUS. The main diagnosis was septic shock (a severe infection that lowers blood pressure and can stop the heart). Secondary diagnoses were heart failure (the heart could not pump enough blood), an abscess in the left thigh (a pocket of pus), osteomyelitis in the pubis (bone infection), Fournier's syndrome (a serious infection of the genital area), chronic kidney disease (long‑term kidney damage), acute dialysis (a temporary kidney replacement), cardiorespiratory arrest (heart and breathing stopped), hyperkalemia (high potassium in the blood), bradycardia (slow heart rate), QRS widening (an abnormal heart rhythm on the ECG), and refractory shock (shock that did not improve with treatment).

When the patient was admitted, the main symptoms were heart failure and an abscess in the left thigh.

The following procedures were carried out: the abscess in the left thigh was drained with ultrasound guidance on 12/03, a drain was placed on 12/15, an incision was made in the intensive care unit (ICU) on 12/17, effective electrical cardioversion (a shock to restore normal rhythm) was performed on 12/17, dialysis was done through a fistula on 12/16, drainage of Fournier's gangrene (the genital infection) was done on 12/03, the patient was intubated (a tube was put into the airway) on 12/17, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was performed on 12/17, and ventilator support (a machine to help breathing) was started on 12/17.

The patient received the following medicines: Dobutamine – helps the heart pump better – given on 12/07 and 12/08; Ceftriaxone – an antibiotic to kill bacteria – given as directed by the culture of the abscess; Polymyxin D – an antibiotic for resistant bacteria – given on 12/15; Amikacin – an antibiotic for bacteria – given on 12/17; Vancomycin – an antibiotic for resistant bacteria – given on 12/17; Calcium gluconate – lowers high potassium – 2 ampoules; Bicarbonate – helps reduce potassium level – 100 ml; Atropine – stops heart slowing – 2 ampoules; Norepinephrine – raises blood pressure – 1.5 mcg/kg/min.

The patient had several abnormal findings: Norepinephrine infusion was 1.5 mcg/kg/min; hyperkalemia (high potassium) was noted, with a normal range of 3.5‑5.0 mmol/L; cardiorespiratory arrest and asystole (no heart activity) were recorded; bradycardia (slow heart rate) and QRS widening (abnormal ECG pattern) were seen; refractory shock (shock that did not improve) was present; purulent secretion (pus) was found; fixed mydriasis (pupils that do not change size) was observed; there were no heart sounds; there were no brainstem reflexes; and the respiratory rate was increased on the ventilator to lower CO₂ and potassium.

The warning signs that were noted were cardiorespiratory arrest, asystole, absence of central pulses, fixed mydriasis, absence of heart sounds, absence of brainstem reflexes, and refractory shock.

The patient died. The death was confirmed by the absence of central pulses, pupils in fixed mydriasis, absence of heart sounds, asystole on the monitor, and absence of brainstem reflexes. The body was released and a death certificate is awaited.
